description.value: This study examined regional gray matter, white matter and cerebrospinal fluid volumes in active heavy drinkers and age- and sex-matched light drinkers, including effects of drinking severity and family history of problem drinking.

spans.text: Within heavy drinkers, volumes were correlated with measures of alcohol consumption and compared as a function of family history of problem drinking.

FHP heavy drinkers have smaller brain volumes compared to family-history-negative (FHN) heavy drinkers

spans.text: (1) long-term heavy drinking is associated with reductions of cortical gray matter and white matter, with greatest reductions in the frontal and parietal lobes; (2) at comparable levels of drinking, active heavily drinking women have greater gray matter and white matter reductions than men; (3) lobar gray and white matter volumes within heavy drinkers are negatively correlated with severity of drinking; and (4) FHP heavy drinkers have smaller brain volumes compared to family-history-negative (FHN) heavy drinkers.

description.value: Observational, cross-sectional study of community-dwelling active heavy drinkers and age- and sex-matched light drinkers.

spans.text: The study received institutional review board approval, and patient informed consent was obtained.

name.value: Effects of heavy drinking on gray matter volumes

definition.value: heavy drinking significantly reduced %GM volumes in all lobes except the frontal lobe

spans.text: The individual ANCOVAs showed that %GM volumes decreased with age in all lobes (all P <0.0001), women had greater %GM volumes than men in all lobes (all P ≤0.004), and that heavy drinking significantly reduced %GM volumes in all lobes (all P ≤0.02) except the frontal lobe ( P =0.35), where contrary to our a priori hypothesis of frontal lobe reduction, smaller, nonsignificant GM reductions were observed.

value: chronic heavy alcohol drinking was associated with significant temporal, parietal and occipital GM loss in both men and women

spans.text: The first major finding is that chronic heavy alcohol drinking was associated with significant temporal, parietal and occipital GM loss in both men and women, largely replicating our previous study in men only ( ).

name.value: Effects of family history of problem drinking on CSF volumes

definition.value: Family history of problem drinking was associated with smaller CSF volumes within heavy drinkers.

value: Within the HDs, there were significant overall main effects of age and family history of problem drinking on CSF volumes.
Heavy drinkers who had at least one parent with problem drinking had significantly smaller %CSF volumes in all lobes except the temporal lobe.
There were no significant effects of family history of problem drinking on GM or WM volumes, nor were there any effects of family history of problem drinking within the LDs.
These results seem to suggest that a positive family history of problem drinking protects against GM and WM loss, as indirectly measured by CSF volumes, once alcohol abuse commences.
